begin.verb type: action — dynamic in every live sense, of starting something (*we begin the meeting*) or of something starting (*the rain began*). Not stative, not linking; the frozen *to begin with* is a sentence adverb, not a working verb.
begin.transitivity: **both** — transitive in sense 1 (*we begin the meeting*, also *begin to study* / *begin studying*), intransitive in sense 2 (*the rain began*, *flu season begins earlier*). The object is optional; *begin with / begin at* take a prepositional phrase, not an object.
begin.passive: **yes** in the transitive sense — *the new wing was begun in 1890*, *the report has been begun but not finished*; it sounds formal, and American speech usually reaches for *started*. No passive of the intransitive *the ceremony had begun*.

countersink.verb type: action — dynamic, a physical shop operation on a hole or a fastener. No stative or linking use; the participle *countersunk* doubles as an ordinary adjective (*a countersunk screw*).
countersink.transitivity: **transitive** in both senses, and the object is obligatory — either the hole (*countersink the pilot holes*) or the fastener (*countersink the bolts*). ✗ *He countersank all morning* is incomplete without one.
countersink.passive: **yes**, and it is the commonest form in shop writing — *every fastener on the panel has been countersunk*, *the holes were countersunk before assembly* (never ✗ *were countersank*). The passive blurs into the adjective: *the screws are countersunk*.

drink.verb type: action — dynamic throughout, from the literal swallowing to the figurative *drink in the view*. No stative or linking use; the intoxicated *he was drunk* is the adjective, not the verb.
drink.transitivity: **both** — transitive with the liquid as object (*she drank the whole bottle*, *he drank in every word*), intransitive in the alcohol sense (*he doesn't drink*, *they drank all through the reception*). The object is optional; *drink to* takes a prepositional phrase.
drink.passive: **yes** in the transitive sense — *the whole bottle was drunk before dinner*, *his words were drunk in by the crowd* (stiff but grammatical). Watch the clash with the adjective: *the wine was drunk* reads as the passive, *the guests were drunk* as intoxication. No passive of intransitive *he doesn't drink*.

ring.verb type: action — dynamic in the bell, phone, and resounding senses; also **linking (copular)** in the fixed *ring true / false / hollow*, where an adjective complement follows instead of an object (*his apology didn't ring true*). The separate encircling verb (*ring, ringed, ringed*) is dynamic too.
ring.transitivity: **both** — intransitive when the bell or phone is the subject (*my phone has rung four times*, *the hall rang with laughter*), transitive when a person rings something (*she rang the doorbell*, *the cashier rang up our groceries*, British *he rang her twice*). The linking *ring true* takes a complement, not an object.
ring.passive: **yes** in the transitive senses — *the bell was rung at noon*, *our groceries were rung up in under a minute*. **No** passive of the intransitive *the phone rang* or of the linking use: ✗ *true was rung by his apology*.

shrink.verb type: action — dynamic, and an ergative pair: the same verb names the change of state (*the sweater shrank*) and the causing of it (*they shrank the logo*). No stative or linking use — *shrunken* is an adjective only, never ✗ *it has shrunken*.
shrink.transitivity: **both** — intransitive when the thing gets smaller or a person recoils (*the lake has shrunk*, *the economy shrank*, *the dog shrank back*, *he never shrinks from a hard conversation*), transitive when someone reduces it (*the company shrinks its inventory*, *they shrank the logo*).
shrink.passive: **yes** in the transitive sense — *the department has been shrunk by half*, *the image was shrunk to fit the label*. No passive of the intransitive *the lake has shrunk*, and none of *shrink from*: ✗ *the conversation was shrunk from*.

sing.verb type: action — dynamic in every sense, whether a voice, a bird, a kettle, or an informer is the subject. No stative or linking use.
sing.transitivity: **both**, and **ditransitive** in one pattern — transitive with the song as object (*she sang the national anthem*), ditransitive with a hearer added (*sing me a lullaby* / *sing a lullaby to me*), intransitive in the bird, informer, and *sing along* senses (*cardinals sing outside the window*, *one of the crew sang*). The object is optional.
sing.passive: **yes**, and it is common — *the anthem was sung by a local choir*, *the lullaby was sung so quietly I almost missed it*. No passive of the intransitive senses: ✗ *it was sung by the kettle*.

sink.verb type: action — dynamic, and an ergative pair: it names the going down (*the ferry sank*) and the sending down (*a torpedo sank the destroyer*). No stative or linking use — *sunken* is an adjective only, as in *a sunken living room*.
sink.transitivity: **both** — intransitive in the downward senses (*stones sink*, *the sun sinks behind the ridge*, *my heart sank*, *the news finally sank in*), transitive in the causative and idiomatic ones (*sank the destroyer*, *sink the posts four feet*, *sank half a million into that restaurant*, *sank the free throw*).
sink.passive: **yes** in the transitive senses — *the destroyer was sunk by a single torpedo*, *two new wells have been sunk since the drought*, *the putt was sunk with two seconds left*. No passive of the intransitive *the ferry sank* or *it took a week to sink in*.

spring.verb type: action — dynamic, of sudden elastic movement (*he sprang out of his chair*), of a mechanism releasing (*the trap sprang*), and of things appearing or originating (*coffee shops have sprung up*, *the project sprang from a conversation*). No stative or linking use.
spring.transitivity: **both** — intransitive in the leap, snap, *spring up*, and *spring from* senses, transitive in *spring a leak*, *spring someone* (get them released), and *spring something on someone* (*they sprang a surprise inspection on the department*).
spring.passive: **restricted** — natural in the surprise and release senses: *a surprise inspection was sprung on the whole department*, *she was sprung from the clinic a day early*. No passive of the intransitive *he sprang out of his chair*, and the fixed *spring a leak* resists it: ✗ *a leak was sprung by the old boat*.

stink.verb type: action in form but **stative in behavior** — it reports an ongoing property (smelling foul, being no good), not an event, so the simple present is the normal tense (*those old sneakers stink*, *our defense stinks this season*) and the progressive is rare in American English: ✗ *the fridge is stinking*.
stink.transitivity: **intransitive** in every core sense — *the whole kitchen stank*, *the movie stank*, and in *stink of* the *of*-phrase is a complement, not an object (*the deal stinks of a payoff*). Only the phrasal *stink up* takes an object: *somebody stank up the break room*.
stink.passive: **no** — the verb is intransitive, so there is nothing to promote: ✗ *the kitchen was stunk*, ✗ *the movie was stunk by the cast*. Only *stink up* passivizes at all, and even that is marginal and informal: ?*the break room was stunk up again*, more naturally *got stunk up*.

swim.verb type: action — dynamic, of moving through water (*I swim laps three mornings a week*) and, figuratively, of being awash (*the plate swam in gravy*) or feeling dizzy (*my head swims*). No stative or linking use.
swim.transitivity: **both** — usually intransitive (*she swam across the lake*, *the room swam for a second*), transitive when the distance or the water crossed is the object (*swim the Channel*, *swim two miles*, *nobody had swum that stretch of river*). The object is optional and only appears in that crossing sense.
swim.passive: **restricted** — possible only in the transitive crossing sense, and mostly in sports writing: *that stretch of river hadn't been swum in years*, *the Channel has been swum by hundreds of people*. No passive of the intransitive uses: ✗ *the lake was swum across by her*, ✗ *the room was swum*.
